lessons.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program
practice: Install Python and set up a project environment you can recreate from scratch. Delete it and rebuild it once, to prove you can.
Write a script that composes three functions and prints intermediate values at each stage.
Copy ten pieces of notation out of any article further along in the curriculum, including one you do not understand at all, and translate each into a full English sentence.
Take one expression with a summation sign and expand it by hand for n = 3, then write the loop that computes it.
lessons.synthesis: Without looking, write the definition of a function in one sentence, then explain why $f \circ g$ and $g \circ f$ are different objects.

lessons.title: Growth, Bounds, and Shape
practice: Compute $\log$ of a product of 200 small probabilities two ways, directly and as a sum of logs, and observe where the direct version underflows.
Convert three published language-model losses into perplexities by hand, then check with code.
Derive the three log rules from the exponent laws on paper, closed book.
Plot $x^2$, $2^x$, and $\log_2 x$ on one axis, then again on a log scale, and write one sentence about what changed.
lessons.synthesis: State from memory why cross-entropy is measured in logs rather than in raw probabilities, and what units the result is in.

lessons.title: Coordinates, Systems, and Arrays

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Solve a 3x3 system by hand, then again with NumPy, and confirm the answers match.
Write the distance function for two points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ without loops, using array operations only.
Take an array of shape [4, 6, 8] and produce every reduction over each axis, predicting each output shape before running it.
Deliberately trigger a silent broadcasting bug, then write the assertion that would have caught it.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a homogeneous system having a nonzero solution says about the columns of its matrix.

lessons.title: Angles and Rotation
practice: Write a function that rotates a 2D point by an angle, then verify that rotating twice equals rotating by the sum.
Compute the cosine of the angle between two random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\mathbb{R}^{10}$, and $\mathbb{R}^{1000}$, a thousand samples each, and plot the three distributions.
Multiply two complex numbers in polar form on paper, then predict where the product lands before plotting it.
Look up how rotary position embeddings rotate a coordinate pair, and identify the angle-addition formula inside it. You will not follow the whole method yet; find the trigonometry.
lessons.synthesis: Explain, without notes, why multiplying by a unit complex number is a rotation.

lessons.title: Limits, Series, and Counting
practice: Compute the derivative of $x^2$ from the difference quotient on paper, then verify numerically with shrinking step sizes and plot the error.
Sum a geometric series by hand, then write the code and check where floating point stops agreeing with the formula.
Simulate 100,000 runs of n coin flips and compare the empirical distribution of successes against the binomial formula.
Find the smallest number of terms of a convergent series that gets you within 1e-6, first by bounding the tail, then by brute force.
lessons.synthesis: State the three conditions for continuity and give a function that fails each one.

lessons.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Clone any interpretability repository, build its environment, and run its smallest example end to end.
Take a script that fails and locate the cause from the traceback alone, without reading the whole file.
Reproduce one figure from a paper you can already partly follow, then list every choice the figure's axes hide.
Plot the same data three ways, one of which is misleading, and write down what makes it misleading.
lessons.synthesis: Describe what you would need to record today so that a number you produce could be regenerated in six months.

lessons.title: Consolidation: The Toolkit

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program
Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Closed book, write out the log rules, the distance formula, the angle-addition formulas, and the definition of a limit. Check them afterwards and mark only what you got wrong.
Build one script that uses material from every lesson so far: read data, transform it with array operations, compute a log-scale quantity, and plot it with labeled axes.
Take the exit criteria from all sixteen articles so far and attempt them cold, in random order. Score yourself before checking.
Rewrite, from memory, the explanation of the one topic you found hardest, then compare against the article and note only the gaps.
lessons.synthesis: Which two topics from this part do you predict you will have forgotten most by the next consolidation? Write them down now; you will check that prediction later.

lessons.title: Vectors, Dot Products, and Maps

revisit.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Implement matrix multiplication with explicit loops, then with array operations, and time both.
Write a function that reports whether a set of vectors is linearly independent, and test it on cases you construct to be dependent.
Take three weight matrices from any pretrained model, print their shapes, and write down which space each maps from and to.
Compute cosine similarity between every pair of a hundred random unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{768}$ and plot the histogram. Predict its center and width first.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why a matrix product is a composition of functions, and why the inner dimensions must agree.

lessons.title: Coordinates and Projection

articles.title: Bases, Coordinates, and Change of Basis

revisit.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Implement the projection of a vector onto a direction and onto the orthogonal complement, and verify the two pieces sum back to the original.
Build a projection matrix for a two-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^5$ and check idempotence numerically.
Rotate a basis, express the same vector in both, and confirm that its norm is unchanged while its coordinates are not.
Implement Gram-Schmidt, then find an input where it loses orthogonality numerically, and compare against a QR routine.
lessons.synthesis: State what it means for a basis to be privileged, and why the residual stream of a transformer is usually said not to have one.

lessons.title: Rank and Eigenstructure
practice: Construct a rank-2 matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{10 \times 10}$ three different ways and confirm the rank numerically each time.
Multiply two random matrices with a thin inner dimension and verify the rank bound empirically.
Diagonalize a small symmetric matrix by hand, then check against a library routine.
Find a real matrix with complex eigenvalues, and show numerically that it rotates a vector rather than scaling it.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why $W_Q W_K^T$ has rank at most the head dimension, and what that limits about what a head can attend to.

lessons.title: Decomposition and Quadratic Forms

articles.title: Quadratic Forms and Positive Semi-Definite Matrices

revisit.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Take the SVD of a weight matrix from a real model, plot the singular value spectrum, and estimate its effective rank.
Truncate that SVD at several ranks, measure reconstruction error, and compare against the Eckart-Young bound.
Generate correlated 2D data, compute its covariance, and plot the covariance ellipse with its principal axes.
Whiten that data and confirm the new covariance is the identity.
lessons.synthesis: Explain the relationship between the SVD, the eigendecomposition of $M^T M$, and the geometry of a quadratic form.

lessons.title: Fitting and Shapes in Code

revisit.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Solve a least-squares problem three ways, by normal equations, QR, and SVD, and compare accuracy on an ill-conditioned input.
Verify numerically that the least-squares residual is orthogonal to the column space.
Write the per-head attention score computation as a single einsum and check the output shape against a loop version.
Take five einsum strings from a real interpretability codebase and read each one aloud as a sentence.
lessons.synthesis: Describe least squares as a projection, naming what is projected onto what.

lessons.title: Many Dimensions, Real Machines

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Verify the concentration of random cosine similarity as dimension grows, and compare against the $1/\sqrt{d}$ prediction.
Count how many vectors you can pack in $\mathbb{R}^{64}$ with pairwise cosine below 0.1, by random search, and compare to the theoretical scaling.
Estimate the memory needed to cache every residual-stream activation for a small model and a batch of 32, then measure it and compare.
Compute the same sum in float32 and bfloat16 with terms in different orders, and record the disagreement.
lessons.synthesis: Explain, with numbers, why a 768-dimensional space can host far more than 768 nearly independent directions.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Linear Algebra

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, reconstruct the relationships between rank, the SVD, projection, and least squares as a single diagram.
Re-attempt the exit criteria from Part 1 and Part 2 together, shuffled, without looking at which lesson each came from.
Take a weight matrix from a real model and produce a one-page analysis: shapes, rank, spectrum, and what the map does.
Check the prediction you wrote at the last consolidation. Were the topics you expected to forget the ones you actually forgot?
lessons.synthesis: Explain the whole of Part 2 to an imagined reader who has finished Part 1 only, in writing, in under 500 words.

lessons.title: Rates of Change
practice: Differentiate ReLU, GELU, sigmoid, and softmax by hand, then verify each numerically by finite differences.
Implement a gradient checker and use it on a two-layer network you write yourself.
Compute the gradient of a scalar function of a 100-dimensional input and confirm the steepest-ascent property empirically.
Take a composition four functions deep and apply the chain rule on paper, tracking every factor.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a directional derivative measures, and what it would mean to take one along a steering vector.

lessons.title: Approximation, Jacobians, and Accumulation
practice: Approximate a nonlinear function at a point to first and second order, and plot where each approximation stops being usable.
Compute a Jacobian for a small vector-valued function, first by hand and then with autodiff, and compare.
Implement integrated gradients for a simple function and verify the completeness property numerically.
Find a case where the first-order estimate of an intervention's effect disagrees badly with the true effect, and explain why.
lessons.synthesis: State exactly which term attribution patching discards, and describe a situation where discarding it is unsafe.

lessons.title: Randomness and Its Moments

articles.title: Conditional Probability, Independence, and Bayes' Rule

practice: Sample from a categorical distribution 100,000 times and confirm the empirical frequencies converge at the rate you predict.
Compute a detector's precision from its true-positive rate, false-positive rate, and a base rate of 1 in 10,000, then argue about whether it is deployable.
Construct two variables that are uncorrelated but strongly dependent, and plot them.
Write out a short sentence's probability under the autoregressive factorization, naming every conditional.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why a probe with 99% accuracy on a rare behavior can be mostly wrong when it fires.

lessons.title: Estimating and Sampling

revisit.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Derive the maximum likelihood estimate for a categorical distribution on paper, then confirm it is the empirical frequency.
Estimate a mean by Monte Carlo at several sample sizes and plot the error against $1/\sqrt{n}$.
Implement temperature, top-k, and top-p sampling from a fixed logit vector, and plot how each reshapes the distribution.
Compare a paired and an unpaired estimate of the same difference, and measure how much variance pairing removed.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why training a language model is maximum likelihood estimation, and what it is estimating.

lessons.title: Structure in Data

revisit.title: Making Code and Figures You Can Trust

practice: Bootstrap a confidence interval for a difference in means and compare it against a t-based interval.
Screen 144 random 'heads' for an effect that does not exist, at alpha 0.05, and count the false positives. Then apply a correction.
Run PCA two ways on the same data, by eigendecomposition of the covariance and by SVD of the centered matrix, and confirm agreement.
Take a high-variance principal component of some real activations and argue both for and against reading it as a concept.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what changes about a dataset's geometry when you whiten it, and why erasure methods care.

lessons.title: Information
practice: Compute entropy, cross-entropy, and KL for several small distributions by hand, then verify with code.
Take a real model's next-token distribution on a few prompts and compute its entropy. Find a prompt where it is very low and one where it is high.
Compute the KL between a model's output and the same model with one component ablated, and compare it against the change in top-1 accuracy.
Demonstrate the asymmetry of KL with a concrete pair of distributions where the two directions differ sharply.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a circuit faithfulness score reported as a KL divergence is actually measuring, and in which direction.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Mathematics

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, write the definitions of expectation, variance, entropy, cross-entropy, and KL, then check.
Shuffle the exit criteria from every mathematics article so far and work through twenty of them at random, scoring yourself before checking.
Take one dataset and produce a single analysis that uses probability, linear algebra, and information theory together.
List the three ideas from Parts 1 to 3 you are least confident about, and schedule them into the practice of the next several lessons.
lessons.synthesis: Write the mathematical prerequisites of mechanistic interpretability as a one-page map, from memory, then compare it against the site's prerequisite links.

lessons.title: Optimization
practice: Implement gradient descent on a badly conditioned quadratic and watch it zig-zag, then fix it with a preconditioner.
Solve a small constrained problem with Lagrange multipliers by hand and interpret the multiplier's value.
Fit the same model with L1 and L2 penalties across a sweep of strengths, and plot the number of nonzero coefficients against the penalty.
Derive the soft-thresholding operator from the L1 proximal problem, then implement ISTA and watch coefficients hit exactly zero.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why an L1-penalized autoencoder systematically underestimates the magnitude of the features it finds.

lessons.title: Cause
practice: Build a three-variable simulation with a confounder, and show that conditioning and intervening give different answers.
Construct a collider and demonstrate that conditioning on it creates a dependence that was not there.
Simulate a mediation setup and estimate the direct and indirect effects, then break the estimate by adding an interaction.
Take a published clean-corrupted prompt pair from any interpretability paper and list everything it fails to hold fixed.
lessons.synthesis: Explain the difference between noising and denoising as mediation questions, and describe a case where they disagree.

lessons.title: Curved Spaces
practice: Sample points from a curved 1D manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{50}$ and estimate its intrinsic dimension two different ways.
Show that PCA fails on that data, and that a nonlinear method recovers the structure.
Move along a great circle on a sphere and compare against moving in a straight line in the ambient space, measuring how far the straight path leaves the surface.
Run t-SNE on the same data with five different perplexity settings and write down which apparent structures survive.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why a steering direction is a tangent vector, and what that predicts about large interventions.

lessons.title: Learning from Data
practice: Fit a logistic regression on synthetic data, then design a control task in the style of Hewitt and Liang and measure selectivity.
Plot ROC and precision-recall curves for the same classifier on a heavily imbalanced dataset, and argue which is honest.
Choose an operating point under a fixed false-positive budget and report the true-positive rate there.
Construct a train and test split that leaks, measure the inflated accuracy, then fix the split and measure again.
lessons.synthesis: Explain precisely what a probe's high accuracy does and does not establish about the model it was trained on.

lessons.title: Networks and Their Gradients
practice: Build a scalar-valued autodiff engine from scratch, then train a small network with it.
Derive the cross-entropy gradient with respect to logits on paper and confirm it numerically.
Demonstrate softmax shift invariance in code, and show why logit differences are the meaningful quantity.
Construct a saturated softmax where a component matters causally but its gradient is near zero.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why reverse-mode differentiation is cheap for a scalar loss, in terms of Jacobian products.

lessons.title: Training at Scale

articles.title: Training Deep Networks: SGD, Adam, and Schedules

practice: Implement Adam from the paper and match a library implementation step for step on the same seed.
Train the same small model with and without a residual connection and compare the gradient magnitudes at the earliest layer.
Implement LayerNorm and RMSNorm, then show how the input-dependent scale breaks an additive decomposition of the residual stream.
Train word embeddings on a small corpus and test the analogy arithmetic, including the cases the critiques say fail.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why layer normalization complicates direct logit attribution, and what freezing it assumes.

lessons.title: Consolidation: From Mathematics to Models

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, draw the path from maximum likelihood to the cross-entropy loss to backpropagation to a weight update.
Take twenty exit criteria drawn at random from Parts 2, 3, and 4 and attempt them in one sitting, mixed.
Train a small network end to end on a real dataset, with a plotted training curve, an error bar, and a held-out evaluation.
Write down which mathematical topic you have now used most often in practice, and which you have not touched since you read it.
lessons.synthesis: Explain, in writing, why a transformer's loss being cross-entropy is a consequence of decisions made in probability theory rather than an arbitrary engineering choice.

lessons.title: Language Models
practice: Implement byte-pair encoding from scratch on a small corpus and inspect the merge list.
Take twenty prompts and find three where tokenization does something surprising, including one number and one rare word.
Train a character-level recurrent model and observe the vanishing gradient on long sequences.
Write the training loss for one specific short sequence, naming every term, then verify against a real model's reported loss.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what causal masking makes impossible, in terms of information flow between positions.

lessons.title: How Chat Models Are Made
practice: Load a base model and its chat counterpart, run the same prompts through both, and catalogue the differences.
Measure the weight-space distance between base and chat, layer by layer, and plot it.
Reproduce a few-shot scaling curve: accuracy against number of demonstrations, on a task you construct.
Design an experiment that separates learning from the demonstrations' content from learning from their format.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what the KL penalty in RLHF prevents, and why refusal being mediated by one direction is surprising given the training procedure.

lessons.title: Representations Worth Learning
practice: Train a linear autoencoder and confirm it recovers the PCA subspace but not PCA's basis.
Generate data from a known sparse dictionary, then try to recover the dictionary and measure how close you got.
Vary the dictionary size on that synthetic data and watch feature splitting appear.
Compute CKA and CCA between two networks trained from different seeds, and explain any disagreement between the measures.
lessons.synthesis: Describe a sparse autoencoder entirely in the vocabulary of dictionary learning, and say what the identifiability results imply about its features.

lessons.title: Instrumenting a Model
practice: Implement activation patching in raw PyTorch with forward hooks, on a small model, with no interpretability library.
Cache every residual-stream activation for a batch, measure the memory used, and compare against your earlier estimate.
Take a gradient with respect to an activation rather than a parameter, and confirm you understand which is which.
Break your own hook deliberately, by removing it too late and by returning the wrong shape, and read each resulting error.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a forward hook is and at what point in the forward pass it fires, without looking it up.

lessons.title: Following a Token Through
practice: Implement a decoder-only transformer forward pass from scratch, small enough to run on a laptop, matching a reference implementation's outputs.
Print the shape of every intermediate tensor for one token's journey through a real model, and label each with the space it lives in.
Compare learned, sinusoidal, and rotary position handling on the same short sequence and describe what each does to the scores.
Take the unembedding matrix of a real model and find the nearest tokens to a few embedding vectors.
lessons.synthesis: Describe the residual stream as a communication channel: who writes to it, who reads from it, and what that buys.

lessons.title: Attention and MLPs
practice: Implement attention from scratch with explicit einsums, and verify against a library implementation on the same weights.
Visualize attention patterns for several heads on a repeated-token sequence and label what each head appears to do.
Find a neuron in a real model that activates on something legible, then find one that clearly does not.
Fold the LayerNorm gain into the adjacent weight matrix and confirm the model's outputs are unchanged.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why layer normalization is the component that breaks the additive decomposition of the residual stream.

lessons.title: Circuits in the Weights
practice: Compute the full $W_Q W_K^T$ and $W_O W_V$ matrices for one head and inspect their rank and spectrum.
Look for evidence of copying by examining the eigenvalues of an OV circuit, and compare across several heads.
Measure composition between a pair of heads in adjacent layers and report which kind you found.
Generate text with greedy, temperature, top-k, and top-p decoding from the same prompt and logits, and describe the differences.
lessons.synthesis: Explain how a head decomposes into a matching circuit and a copying circuit, and what each is a function of.

lessons.title: Consolidation: The Architecture

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, draw a full transformer block with every tensor shape labeled, then check it against your own implementation.
Attempt exit criteria from Parts 4 and 5 mixed together, including at least five from the mathematics parts.
Take your from-scratch transformer and add one instrumentation feature: cache an activation of your choice and plot it across layers.
Re-read only the notes you took, not the articles, and list what your notes fail to capture.
lessons.synthesis: Explain to an imagined reader who knows the mathematics but has never seen a transformer what the architecture computes and why the residual stream matters.

lessons.title: What the Field Is Claiming
practice: Reproduce a toy model of superposition: train a small autoencoder-like model on sparse features and observe the packing.
Vary sparsity in that toy model and plot when superposition appears and when it does not.
Find a polysemantic neuron in a real model and document three unrelated things it fires on.
Write the strongest argument you can against the linear representation hypothesis, then the strongest defense.
lessons.synthesis: State the superposition hypothesis precisely enough to be tested, and name the evidence that would refute it.

lessons.title: Reading the Model's Mind

articles.title: The Logit Lens and Tuned Lens

practice: Implement the logit lens on a real model and plot how the predicted token changes across layers for several prompts.
Train a tuned lens probe for one layer and compare its predictions against the raw logit lens.
Decompose a logit difference into per-head contributions and rank the heads.
Find a prompt where the logit lens is misleading, and explain what the tuned lens fixes.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what direct logit attribution measures, and name one thing it systematically misses.

lessons.title: Causal Intervention
practice: Run activation patching across every layer and position for one behavior, and produce the standard heatmap.
Run the same experiment in both the noising and the denoising direction and compare the results.
Design three different corrupted prompts for the same clean prompt and show how the conclusion changes.
Patch at the level of a head, a neuron, and a learned direction on the same behavior, and compare what each tells you.
lessons.synthesis: Explain which mediation estimand your patching experiment computed, and what assumption it relies on.

lessons.title: Attribution at Scale
practice: Implement attribution patching and compare its estimates against true activation patching on the same components.
Find the components where the two disagree most, and explain the disagreement from the Taylor expansion.
Implement an integrated-gradients variant and check whether the disagreement shrinks.
Ablate a component known to matter and measure whether later components compensate.
lessons.synthesis: Explain how self-repair can make a genuinely important component look unimportant.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Techniques

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, list every technique so far for asking what a component does, and give one weakness of each.
Take one behavior in one model and attack it with three different methods, then write up where they agree and disagree.
Attempt a mixed set of exit criteria from Parts 3, 5, and 6, without checking which lesson each came from.
Return to the toy superposition model from earlier and apply a technique you have learned since.
lessons.synthesis: Write the case for and against the claim that activation patching establishes causation in a neural network.

lessons.title: Probing

articles.title: Truthfulness Probing and the Geometry of Truth

practice: Train linear probes at every layer for one property and plot accuracy across depth.
Add a control task and report selectivity alongside accuracy.
Train an attention probe and compare it against mean pooling on the same task.
Reproduce a truth-direction result on a small model, then test whether the direction transfers to a different dataset.
lessons.synthesis: Explain the gap between a property being linearly decodable and the model actually using it.

lessons.title: Directions from Contrast
practice: Compute a contrastive activation direction from many pairs and measure how the direction stabilizes as pairs are added.
Compare that direction against a trained probe's weight vector by cosine similarity.
Take a probe validated on one dataset and evaluate it on a genuinely different distribution, reporting the drop.
Build a two-stage cascade and measure the cost saving against the accuracy loss.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a contrastive steering vector estimates, in the language of expectations.

lessons.title: Steering
practice: Add a steering vector at several layers and strengths, and map the region where behavior changes without fluency collapsing.
Ablate the same direction and compare what disappears against what addition produced.
Show that projecting out a direction does not remove the information, by training a fresh probe on the projected activations.
Implement affine steering with a recentering term and compare against plain addition.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why ablating a direction is weaker evidence of erasure than it first appears.

lessons.title: Learned and Distributed Control
practice: Extract a task vector from in-context examples and test whether it transfers to a zero-shot prompt.
Optimize a steering vector under a norm constraint without labels, and inspect what behavior it produces.
Distribute a fixed steering budget across layers in several ways and compare robustness.
Use a probe's output as a training signal on a small fine-tune and measure what it changed.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why an unsupervised steering method can surface behaviors the researcher did not think to look for.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Control

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, write the taxonomy of interventions you now know: what each does to an activation, and what each licenses you to claim.
Take a single concept and attack it with a probe, a contrastive vector, ablation, and patching, then write up the four results together.
Mixed retrieval across Parts 5 and 6, at least twenty items, scored before checking.
Check your earlier prediction about which topics you would forget. Update how you allocate revisiting.
lessons.synthesis: Write the strongest version of the claim that steering demonstrates a representation is causally used, then the strongest objection to it.

lessons.title: Editing Weights

articles.title: Localized Fact Editing and Its Pitfalls

practice: Implement a rank-one weight edit that inserts a fact, and test generalization to paraphrases.
Show that a successful edit does not prove the fact was stored where you edited.
Implement LEACE on real activations and confirm that a linear probe can no longer recover the concept.
Then train a nonlinear probe on the same erased activations and report what remains.
lessons.synthesis: Explain precisely what LEACE's guarantee covers and what it does not.

lessons.title: Sparse Autoencoders
practice: Train a small sparse autoencoder on activations you collect yourself, and plot the sparsity-fidelity frontier across penalty strengths.
Measure dead features and implement one resampling strategy, then measure again.
Build a feature dashboard for ten of your features: top activating examples, logit effects, and activation histogram.
Write your own label for five features, then compare against an automated explanation, and note where they disagree.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a sparse autoencoder assumes about how features are represented, and what happens when that assumption fails.

lessons.title: Scaling and Variants
practice: Train TopK and JumpReLU variants on the same activations and compare their frontiers against your L1 baseline.
Evaluate all three by substituting the reconstruction back into the model and measuring loss recovered, not just reconstruction error.
Clamp a feature to a large value and observe the behavioral change, then try to break the effect.
Explore a large public SAE on Neuronpedia and find one feature whose published label you disagree with.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why downstream loss recovered is a better evaluation than reconstruction MSE.

lessons.title: Beyond the Residual Stream
practice: Train a transcoder to replace one MLP and measure how much of the layer's behavior it preserves.
Train a crosscoder across two adjacent layers and inspect which features are shared and which are layer-specific.
Compare a token-wise feature dictionary against one trained on span-averaged activations.
Take a feature you found earlier and track it across layers with your crosscoder.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a transcoder buys for circuit analysis that a residual-stream SAE does not.

lessons.title: The Shape of Features
practice: Find a set of features that form a discrete category and test whether they occupy a simplex-like arrangement.
Look for a periodic feature, such as days or months, and check whether it traces a circle.
Estimate the intrinsic dimension of the activations for a constrained family of prompts.
Steer along a straight line and along a curved path fitted to the manifold, and compare fluency at large step sizes.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why some concepts cannot be captured by a single direction, with a concrete example.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Decomposition

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, list every decomposition method you know, what it decomposes, and what it assumes.
Take one model and one concept and find it three ways: a probe, an SAE feature, and a contrastive direction. Compare the three objects.
Mixed retrieval drawing on Parts 4, 6, and 7, at least twenty items.
Return to sparse coding theory and re-read only your notes, then say what the identifiability results predict about your own SAE's features.
lessons.synthesis: Write the case that sparse autoencoders find the model's features, and the case that they find a convenient basis that merely reconstructs well.

lessons.title: Comparing Models
practice: Take a base and a fine-tuned model and amplify their logit difference to surface a rare behavior.
Train a crosscoder across the two models and find features present in one but not the other.
Build the control that distinguishes a genuine model difference from a sparsity artifact, and run it.
Probe for the fine-tuning domain in the activations of the fine-tuned model and measure how detectable it is.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a base-versus-chat comparison controls for, and what confounds remain.

lessons.title: Induction and a First Circuit

articles.title: The IOI Circuit: Discovery and Mechanism

practice: Measure induction behavior on repeated random token sequences and find the heads responsible.
Trace the previous-token head and the induction head, and demonstrate the composition between them.
Reproduce the indirect object identification circuit on GPT-2 small, at least as far as identifying the name mover heads.
Find a prompt where the circuit you traced fails, and explain why.
lessons.synthesis: Explain how two heads compose into a pattern-copying mechanism, in terms of QK and OV circuits.

lessons.title: Evaluating a Circuit

articles.title: Circuit Evaluation: Faithfulness, Completeness, and Minimality

practice: Take your IOI circuit and test faithfulness, completeness, and minimality, reporting each number.
Find the negative contributors and show what happens to your metrics when they are removed.
Design an entity-binding prompt set and test which of the competing retrieval mechanisms your model uses.
Find a copy-suppression head and demonstrate its effect on a token repeated from context.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why a circuit can be faithful and still not be an explanation.

lessons.title: Feature-Level Circuits
practice: Build an attribution graph over transcoder features for one prompt and read off the main path.
Validate one edge of that graph with a direct intervention, and report whether it held.
Compare a circuit you found in two models trained from different seeds, using a similarity measure you can defend.
Take one text-model technique and apply it to a vision-language model, and report what transferred.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a replacement model is, and the ways an attribution graph over one can mislead.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Mechanism

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, write the full pipeline from a behavior to a validated circuit, naming the method used at each step.
Take a behavior nobody has published a circuit for and get as far as a defensible hypothesis, documenting dead ends.
Mixed retrieval across Parts 5 through 8, at least twenty-five items.
Compare your current notes against the notes you took in Part 5, and rewrite one early note now that you know more.
lessons.synthesis: Write an honest account of what the field can and cannot currently establish about a circuit, using your own experiments as evidence.

lessons.title: Weights Rather Than Activations
practice: Decompose a small model's weights into rank-one subcomponents and ablate the ones the model does not use on a task.
Compare a circuit found in parameter space against one found in activation space for the same behavior.
Prune a subnetwork without an adversary, then with one, and compare the sizes you get.
Train a tiny weight-sparse model and read a circuit directly off its weights.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why pruning without an adversary understates the size of a circuit.

lessons.title: Decoding Hidden States

articles.title: Hidden State Decoding: From Vectors to Language

practice: Patch a hidden state into an explanatory prompt and get a natural-language description out.
Design the control that checks whether the description tracks the activation rather than the surrounding prompt.
Compare a patchscope description against what the logit lens says about the same state.
Find a case where the description is fluent and confident and also wrong.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what makes a self-report about an activation evidence, rather than a plausible confabulation.

lessons.title: Trained Interpreters

articles.title: Training Models to Explain Their Computations

practice: Inject a known concept into a hidden state and test whether the model's self-report tracks the injection.
Run the control where the concept is absent but the prompt suggests it, and compare.
Train a small decoder to answer questions about activations, and evaluate it on held-out question types.
Test your decoder on a model organism it never saw during training.
lessons.synthesis: Explain the difference between a model reporting its internal state and a model producing a plausible answer about it.

lessons.title: Open-Ended Interpretation
practice: Evaluate an activation interpreter across several question types and report where it degrades.
Train a verbalizer and reconstructor pair and measure whether the explanation retains enough to reconstruct.
Take a chain-of-thought trace and resample after each step to measure which steps the answer depends on.
Find a reasoning trace where the stated reasoning and the causally load-bearing steps differ.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what counterfactual resampling establishes about a reasoning trace that reading it cannot.

lessons.title: Consolidation: The Whole Method

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Closed book, reconstruct the site's three textbooks as a single map, from notation to safety applications.
Take one open question in interpretability and write a research proposal: hypothesis, method, controls, and what would falsify it.
Mixed retrieval across every part so far, at least thirty items, drawn at random.
Identify the three articles you have used most in practice and the three you have never returned to, and ask why.
lessons.synthesis: Write, from memory, the strongest critique of mechanistic interpretability as a research program that you can honestly make.

lessons.title: Detection

articles.title: Detecting Sleeper Agents with Mechanistic Interpretability

practice: Find and validate a refusal direction on an open chat model, and test it causally in both directions.
Train a probe on a model organism with a known backdoor and report its operating point under a realistic false-positive budget.
Evaluate that probe on a behavior it was not trained on, and report the drop.
Write down what result would convince you that a detector works on deception rather than on a proxy.
lessons.synthesis: Explain why detecting a trained backdoor is weaker evidence than detecting emergent deception, and what the gap consists of.

lessons.title: Monitoring and Its Limits

articles.title: Understanding Safety Mechanisms and MI-Based Monitoring
Limits of Mechanistic Interpretability for Safety

practice: Test whether a model behaves differently on prompts that look like evaluations, and quantify the difference.
Design a monitoring setup with an explicit false-positive budget and estimate its cost at deployment scale.
Take one published safety-relevant interpretability result and write the strongest critique of its evaluation.
List the failure modes of your own experiments from earlier parts that this article names.
lessons.synthesis: Explain how evaluation awareness could invalidate a safety measurement, and what design would detect it.

lessons.title: The Tooling
practice: Redo one experiment you previously wrote in raw PyTorch using TransformerLens, and compare the code.
Do the same experiment again in nnsight, and write down which abstraction suited it better.
Train or load an SAE with SAE Lens and connect its features to Neuronpedia.
Verify one library's convenience function against your own implementation, and find any discrepancy.
lessons.synthesis: Explain what a hook-based library is doing on your behalf, and how you would check it.

lessons.title: Becoming a Researcher
practice: Work through the ARENA sections covering material you found hardest, not the ones you found easy.
Pick one paper you now believe is wrong or overstated, and write the rebuttal with your own evidence.
Write up one of your earlier experiments as a short public post, with methods, results, and limitations.
Identify three open problems you could plausibly attack, and write one paragraph on each.
lessons.synthesis: Write the research agenda you would pursue, and what you would need to learn next that this site does not cover.

lessons.title: Capstone: An Original Investigation

revisit.title: Notation, Functions, and a First Program

practice: Choose a behavior in a real model that nobody has explained, and investigate it end to end: hypothesis, method, controls, negative results, and a falsifiable claim.
Use at least three different techniques and report where they disagree.
Have the whole thing reviewed by someone who will push back, and revise it.
Final mixed retrieval across the entire curriculum, drawn at random, scored honestly before checking.
lessons.synthesis: Write the account of what you now know that you could not have written at the start, and be specific about which parts of the plan produced it.
